# Fae · Book II, pp. 94–115
# Generated by the extractor — fix the extractor, not this file.
PAGE	94
P	Strange folk live in the <b>Great Wood</b> (page 200) and <b>Ferrier's Fen</b> (page 116).
P	Wondrous and dangerous, beings out of legend. The <b>Forest Folk</b> (page 150) called them "Good Neighbors" and "Hidden Ones," and took pains to avoid insulting them. They cautioned Stonetop to do the same. And while the Forest Folk are gone, the Fae remain.
P	The <b>Green Lords</b> (page 210) bred the Fae long ago, to herd spirits and to weave wondrous realms. They relied on the Fae to manage their estates, to build the <b>waystones</b> (page 478), and, later, to create the Green Lord's idyllic afterlives.
P	Some Fae resented their servitude. Some found loopholes in the promises and oaths that bound them. Ringleaders arose, creating webs of debt and obligation that undermined their masters' hold.
P	An uprising began. Rebels gutted tombs, burned plantations, put their masters to the spear. Gangs of free Fae roved the Great Wood, burning, liberating, recruiting. Gangs became armies.
P	The Green Lords grew desperate. They called on the <b>Things Below</b> (page 412), corrupted themselves with unholy power.
P	They bred living weapons, hunted down the rebels, and took terrible vengeance.
P	The uprising nearly failed, but the Green Lords had drawn the ire of their fellow
P	Makers. The <b>Stone Lords</b> (page 382), in particular, were horrified by the Green Lords' corruption. They worked a terrible spell to shatter the heart of the Green Lord's domain, turning it into the ruined bog that today we call Ferrier's Fen. Then they allied with the Fae, and waged war against the Green Lords who survived.
P	After the siege of <b>Vor Svetelik</b> (page 468), the Fae found themselves adrift and bereft of purpose. Many were no longer bound by oath or obligation. Ringleaders bickered and squabbled. Factions formed.
P	Armies disbanded. And the Fae became the fractured people they are today.
PAGE	95
H2	The good neighbors
HR
P	Fae and mortals cross paths, of course. The Forest Folk descended from the Green Lord's mortal servants, and dwelt in the Great Wood for centuries. Fae fought side-by-side with the Stone Lords' human slaves. And some Fae, certainly, know of the humans living on their borders: Stonetop, <b>Marshedge</b> (page 274), the <b>Manmarchers</b> (page 282), even some <b>Whitefang villages</b> (page 483). There have always been dealings between them and us.
P	But Fae are not like us. They breathe magic. Time means little to them. They have no base needs. They are driven by pride, boredom, and obsession. They are shaped by their debts, their obligations, and the ancient scars of servitude and war.
P	Fae are <i>dangerous</i> to mortals. Maybe not hostile (though some are), but alien. Some admire our spark of life, our creativity and passion. Some find our memories and our emotions rich and heady. Some delight in our dignity or our short-lived antics. Some might even care about us. But they also think no more of stealing an infant from the crib than we would at picking a pup out of a litter.
H3	The Fae
H2	Themes
HR
P	Choose or roll 1 (or 2 and combine).
P	1d12 theme
HR
P	1 Fluidity of time and space: stasis, distortion, dilation, things where (and when) they oughtn't be
P	2 Enchantment, dreams and dreamlogic, the odd accepted as normal
P	3 Illusion/glamour, often hiding a base or even sordid reality
P	4 The intangible made real; metaphor made literal
P	5 Promises, deals, and loopholes; debts and insults weighing heavy as iron chains
P	6 Opaque etiquette, strange norms, values upended, seeming amorality
P	7 Passions, whims, and excess; the autonomy of others ignored
P	8 Extremes of beauty/ugliness, blurred lines between them
P	9 Malleability of one's looks, one's identity, one's true and secret heart
P	10 Liminality: neither spirit nor flesh, here nor there, this nor that, real nor unreal
P	11 Deep ties to the natural world and <b>spirits of the wild</b> (page 356)
P	12 Enslavement by the <b>Green Lords</b> (page 210), the war against them, the lasting scars left by both

H2	Hooks
HR
B	A local family claims their infant has been replaced with a Fae changeling.
B	A widower wants a Fae to take away the memories of his lost love.
B	A hunter naively offers Stonetop's hospitality to a mischievous Fae.
B	A <b>zrajedak</b> (page 223) is released from stasis; terrified Fae seek help.
B	An NPC is indebted to a Fae; it wants what they cannot bear to give (a child, their love, a marriage, etc.).
B	A Fae falls in love with a villager, and tries to live a mortal life.
H2	Questions
HR
P	In general:
Q	Who among you has lost a sibling or a child, stolen from the crib?
Q	Who in the village is said to have Fae blood?
Q	Who in town once made a deal with a Fae? What did they lose? What did they get in return?
Q	What Fae being did you once meet in the Wood? How did you get away unscathed?
P	About any given Fae they meet:
Q	What about their presence fills you with awe/longing/sadness/joy/__?
Q	What forgotten memory do they stir?
Q	What detail about them will you struggle to remember later?
Q	What detail could you never forget?

B	Strange, magical folk dwell in the Great Wood
B	They vary greatly in appearance, ability, and disposition
B	That they are strange, dreamlike, fickle, wondrous, dangerous

B	That iron is anathema to them
B	Proper etiquette for dealing with one
B	Ways to protect yourself from them
B	About domains: their entrances, the dangers they pose, specific examples
B	Tales of the Wandering Market
B	That they served the Green Lords
P	Very few know:
B	The specifics of their history, their origin, their rebellion
B	The nuances of their politics, debts, relationships, obligations
B	How to find the Wandering Market
B	The metaphysics of their existence

H2	Names
HR
P	Fae "names" tend to be titles, nouns, or descriptive phrases or borrowed from those they've met—simple, whimsical, ominous, or grandiose as befits their nature.
P	Mix, match, and riff on words related to plants and beasts and rocks, features of the landscape, natural phenomena, colors, mundane objects, emotions or emotional activities, titles, relations, and local names.
P	Some simple names: Acorn, Cobweb, Hob, Jackdaw, Kettle, Lark, Moth, Quills, Rill, Robin, Stewpot, Trillium, Uncle Whiskers, Whistler, Wobbles, Yellowtail Some whimsical names: Bellweather, Bitterlips, Moonbeam, Peasebottom, Poppy o' Twilight, Rainpetal, Stagthorn, Thistledust, Whiteoak, Yellow Britches
P	Some ominous names: Bonekettle, Father
P	Longfingers, Grinning Nel, the Hangman, the King of Dirges, Old Sorrows, the Pale Sisters, Stonetooth, the Weeping Rose Some grandiose names: Dawnwhisper, Fireblossom, Breath of Thunder, Hare
P	Starblade, the Midnight Mare, Rain Upon the Valley, Silverstag, the Storm King Some Fae might go by many names, or change their names over time. If a given
P	Fae is known to the locals, consider what they call it in their local tongue. A Fae named Moonbeam, for example, might be called "Pelydrlloer" in Stonetop or "Mondstrohl" by the Manmarchers.
P	Perhaps each Fae has a true and secret name, by which they can be commanded and bound. If so, it must be their most treasured and precious secret.
PAGE	98
HR
P	The Fae are living beings made of spirit-stuff. They aren't quite spirits, but interact with spirits as if they were. They're made of flesh and bone, or close enough, but it is strange, malleable, and resilient. They…
E	need not eat or drink, but can enjoy such fare;
E	need not sleep, but often choose to;
E	can suffocate or drown, but usually recover when they can breathe again;
E	feel no drive to reproduce, but might enjoy sex, fall in love, sire or bear children, steal them from mortals;
E	do not grow feeble with age, but can grow bored, deeply set in their ways;
E	cannot break a promise or an oath, but are keen at finding loopholes; and
E	feel the weight of debts and insults as though they were heavy chains.
H3	Injury
P	Fae are unnaturally tough (Armor 4) and can heal any wound not caused by iron. A Fae who suffers a "mortal" wound might pass through the Last Door. But they might also change their mind and come back later, for Fae are fickle things.
H3	Iron
P	Iron (including steel) is offensive to Fae.
P	Its presence insults them. It disrupts their magic. It burns their skin, ignores their Armor, leaves scars that never fade. Iron can kill a Fae, truly kill them dead.
P	<b>Black iron</b> (page 307) is even worse. Its presence unravels their magic. Its touch doesn't just burn, it suppurates their flesh (+1d6 damage, ignores armor, messy). It leaves vicious, gaping wounds that never heal and that eventually turn them into <b>Hollow Fae</b> (page 114).
H3	Magic and the Fae
P	Fae are Fae, neither spirit nor mortal. As a rule, magic that specifically affects "spirits" or "mortals" does not apply to the Fae. They are their own thing.
P	With that said, magic is fuzzy and each Fae is unique. When in doubt, consider what feels right in this particular case. A ploy that would work in a fairy tale should probably work against the Fae!
H3	Illusions and glamours
P	Illusions are lies. They have no substance.
P	An illusionary chair bears no weight; the illusion of a sword does not cut. A skillful Fae might create the illusion of pain and blood when you are cut with an illusionary sword, but the wound has no lasting effect.
P	Glamour is more profound. It changes a thing and how it interacts with the world, at least until the glamour fades. Glamour a rock into a chair and sit comfortably.
P	Glamour a stick into a sword and it will cut, make you bleed real blood. When the glamour ends, the wound remains.
P	Glamours are like poetry. One might glamour an acorn into a gem, or fluttering leaves into butterflies, or a braying mortal's head into that of a donkey. But one does not just, say, glamour a spear into a puddle of water. These things must rhyme!
P	Fae can see through each other's illusions and glamours, but as a rule they play along.
P	Doing otherwise can be insulting.
P	Glamour affects neither iron nor steel, and the touch of either causes illusions to flicker and fade. The touch of <b>black iron</b> (page 307) dispels both illusions and glamours, like soap dropped in oily water.
PAGE	99
H3	Language
P	Fae understand anyone they meet, and can always make themselves understood. Many speak in an affected manner (accented, in verse, with odd sentence construction, etc.) to amuse themselves, to annoy others, or because that's just how they think.
H3	Debts and promises
P	Fae are bound by debts, obligations, and promises. This applies to mortals who treat with them, too. A Fae might:
P	• Make an offer (fair or lopsided)
P	• Politely decline or dissemble
P	• Insist, ask for more, offer less
P	• Call in a debt, use it as leverage
P	• Make or demand a promise
P	• Find/exploit a loophole
P	• Trade a debt to another Fae
P	When a <b><i>Fae is beholden to you</i></b>, you have advantage on any roll to resist or defend yourself against it. When you <b><i>leverage a debt that they owe you or a</i></b> <b><i>promise they've made</i></b>, gain advantage to Persuade or otherwise influence it.
P	When you <b><i>are beholden to a Fae</i></b>, you have disadvantage on any roll made directly against them (including damage rolls). When you <b><i>fail to uphold a</i></b> <b><i>promise you've made to a Fae</i></b>, for any reason, either you are beholden to that Fae or they take it as an insult (their choice).
P	When you <b><i>pass through the Last</i></b> <b><i>Door</i></b>, all debts you owe and promises you have made are null and void.
H3	Insults and etiquette
P	Fae are also bound by insults, pride, and etiquette. An insulted Fae feels the need for satisfaction like a mortal feels hunger, as a gnawing and physical thing. Their culture is full of little rules and points of etiquette that mortals often stumble over.
P	One might insult a Fae by…
E	rudely refusing an offer;
E	failing to honor a debt or promise;
E	taking what they think they own;
E	making demands or threats without the proper leverage;
E	sneaking iron into their presence;
E	failing to play along with their games;
E	disparaging their honor/their power/ their cunning/whatever they value about themselves; or
E	accusing them of any of the above.
P	When the PCs deal with a Fae, that Fae might:
P	• Set the PCs up for a faux pas
P	• Make an accusation
P	• Act affronted, genuinely or as a ploy
P	• Truly take insult
P	And if insulted, they might:
P	• Demand satisfaction
P	• Storm/scamper off
P	• Offer their forgiveness, as a gift
P	• Ignore all other rules of etiquette
P	• Spread tales or rumors
P	• Hold a grudge, lay plans for revenge
P	• Resort to violence or magic

H2	Fae domains
HR
P	Fae domains are hidden realities, existing between the physical and spirit worlds, touching and overlapping both but part of neither. Some are tiny, intimate, cozy.
P	Others are vast and grand.
P	Not every place where a Fae dwells is truly a domain. Plenty of Fae squat in ruins or caves or hollow trees, perhaps spruced up with glamour but fully in this world.
P	Domains are different, set apart.
P	To create a Fae domain, start with the real-world terrain it borders or overlaps with. Most are found in the <b>Great Wood</b> (page 200), in the <b>Foothills</b> (page 144), or in <b>Ferrier's Fen</b> (page 116); those in the Fen are often <b>corrupted</b> (page 430). Many are part of <b>Green Lord ruins</b> (page 214).
P	Once the real-world terrain is established, pick or roll for its entrance. Interpret the result in light of where it's found.
P	1d6 entrance
HR
P	1 A shimmer, a feeling, little more
P	2 Megalith(s)/a <b>waystone</b> (page 478)
P	3 A door/gate/opening, natural or made, literal or just an impression
P	4 A ring of toadstools or some other distinctive pattern of flora (perhaps <b>useful or valuable</b>, page 458)
P	5 A path/a climb/a descent/a fall
P	6 Only active at certain times (in moonlight, at sunset, in winter, etc.) and roll again If an entrance in the Great Wood is at least 10 years old, it's likely to be marked by Forest Folk <b>glyphs</b> (page 152).
P	For the domain itself, pick or roll for a theme (page 95), the domain's original purpose, the anchor that maintains it, and 1-2 elements. Maybe roll 1d6 to inform its size and scale.
P	1d6 purpose
HR
P	1 Containment: to imprison/preserve
P	2 Habitat: where Fae live/work/play
P	3 Community: a place to gather, trade, gossip, show off, travel
P	4 Status: a monument, a place to impose, someone showing off
P	5 Creativity: an expression, an exploration, a work of art
P	6 Pleasure: a paradise, a retreat, a false afterlife, a playground
PAGE	103
P	1d6 anchor
HR
P	1 The will of a single potent Fae
P	2 The instinct or intent of multiple
P	Fae, dwelling (trapped?) within
P	3 A shard of power left by a powerful
P	Fae, buried or hidden away
P	4 One or more Fae, bound/inert, their essence sunk into the domain
P	5 Rune-carved stone infused with Fae power, a work of the Green Lords
P	6 Roll again, but it's failing, fickle, unstable, possibly abandoned
HR
P	<i>The PCs are exploring a Green Lord's tomb, approaching the burial vault in which the</i> <i>mummified Maker lies. Its spirit lingers on in a Fae domain.</i>
P	<i>The terrain is established (the inside of the tomb). I choose a "door/gate/opening" for the</i> <i>entrance and the purpose is clearly "pleasure… a false afterlife." I roll a 5 for theme</i> <i>("promises, deals, and loopholes…") and a 5 for the anchor ("rune-covered stone"). For</i> <i>elements, I get 6 ("decay/squalor/disorder") and 5 ("a vast and shifting place").</i>
P	<i>despondent Fae servants, bound by ancient oaths. An endless series of dusty halls, rooms and</i> <i>feral gardens, full of discarded wealth and surly Fae avoiding their master. The Green Lord's</i> <i>soul swings from boredom to manic fits, during which whatever Fae is at hand conjures</i>
HR
P	1d6 element
HR
P	1 Exit(s) to <b>Fae paths</b> (page 478) or far-off place(s) in the world
P	2 Surreal landscapes: a forest cave, an underwater kingdom, a castle in the clouds, a tiny place made large, a mundane place made giant, etc.
P	3 "Civilized" things, out of place: a feast hall in a mire, a house carved from a tree, a library in a cave, etc.
P	4 A real place, plucked from the world and the passing of time
P	5 A vast and shifting place, easy to get lost in, always something new
P	6 Decay/squalor/disorder, perhaps hidden by glamour or illusion
P	Populate the domain with Fae and other inhabitants that make sense. Also fill it with <b>artifacts</b> (page 108), and any domain <b>hazards</b> (page 110) that make sense.
P	<b>Time dilation</b> (page 105) is a particular concern to mortal visitors!
P	<i>The theme and elements prompt me to rethink the anchor. The domain is barely maintained by</i> <i>threadbare glamours of the Green Lord's half-remembered deeds. An eternal paradise, indeed.</i>
PAGE	104
H3	Entering domains
P	Some entrances work only at particular times: under a full moon, during winter, at sunrise or sunset, etc. This holds true for both Fae and mortal alike.
P	Otherwise, Fae can freely use the entrance of most domains, like you or I might open a door. For mortals, it's more involved.
P	<b>Something interesting:</b> A mortal might blunder into a Fae domain by accident, or follow a guide, or be drawn into one by a mischievous or malevolent Fae. Or they might fall asleep near an entrance and visit the domain in their dreams. Iron or steel might protect you, or not; you might just find that all your iron was left behind in the world.
P	<b>Something useful:</b> To enter a Fae domain on purpose, you must leave behind all iron and steel, plus one of the following:
B	Follow the footsteps of a Fae guide
B	Addle (open?) your mind with drugs/ alcohol/madness/intense emotion/etc.
B	Have Fae blood in your veins
B	Be able to see through Fae magic and glamours, via <b>Old Mother's Wine</b> (page 509) or a similar effect
H3	Locked entrances
P	Some entrances have special requirements to open them, for both Fae and mortal alike. These requirements might involve…
E	singing/reciting/inscribing the proper words;
E	doing something dangerous, without flinching (like running at the wall);
E	doing something daft (like spinning 'til you fall);
E	paying the toll (a secret, a story, a thing of beauty, a promise, etc.);
E	convincing the guardians to let you in;
E	some variation or combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.
P	The residents of a domain might ignore the requirements of a locked entrance; the creator of a domain almost certainly can.
HR
P	<i>I think my Green Lord's afterlife must</i> <i>certainly be locked. I imagine a grand</i> <i>archway with a pair of powerful Fae</i> <i>guardians watching over it, demanding</i> <i>a toll: none can enter without giving an</i> <i>oath of good behavior.</i>

B	Enchanting, entrancing beauty
B	Time passing unnoticed
B	Dramatic, rugged, strange landscapes

B	Getting lost
B	Capricious weather
B	<b>Elemental spirits</b> (page 360), awake and active and full of opinions
B	<b>Illusions and glamours</b> (page 98)
B	Not being able or allowed to leave

H3	Fluid time
P	Time passes strangely in Fae domains, when it passes at all. Upon returning to the world, one might find that no time has passed, or that time has passed normally, or that they've lost days, weeks, months, or years. Tales tell of folk returning to the world centuries later and crumbling into dust, but those are just tales. Right?
P	Lost time most often afflicts those who:
B	Eat Fae food or drink Fae drink
B	Fall asleep
B	Lose themselves to revels, work, etc.
B	Insult/become indebted to the locals
B	Disrupt a place held in stasis Threaten PCs with lost time, for sure. Use it to explain the absence of PCs whose players have to miss some sessions. But don't have the PCs lose years or decades unless you—and your players—really want to shake up your game.
H3	Some Fae domains
B	A little door in a rocky outcrop, leading to a dying crystal city of tiny Fae and their talking vole subjects.
B	A natural arch of hawthorne trees. Beyond: a tree-lined hall, a runecarved hearth, endless drink & dance.
B	A knot in a large dead tree. One must recite a certain poem to enter. Inside is a crowded theater, where callous Fae call up long-dead shades to play out their mortal dramas.
B	A <b>waystone</b> (page 478) in the mire. A crossroad of many Fae paths, oftused but one must pay a toll of beauty to the wretched troll who guards it.
B	A wide stream. Fall face-first into it and enter a watery, dreamlike realm. A catfish-like Fae arranges stones, treasures, and lost memories into a beautiful, ever-shifting mosaic.
B	A circle of menhirs, entwined in thorns. Can only be entered in moonlight. Inside, all the stones but one are revealed to be <b>Forest Folk</b> (page 150), bound in agony.
PAGE	106
H2	The Wandering Market
HR
P	Little ties the Fae together, except for a desire to show off. And for that, they need an audience. A place to meet and gather. A place to trade stories and wonders and lies.
P	They need the Wandering Market.
H3	Questions
Q	According to tales, when does the Wandering Market convene?
Q	If you could purchase any treasure from the Fae, one wondrous thing, what would it be?
Q	What is your single most treasured possession? Why do you value it so?
Q	Who among you is most beautiful? Has the best singing voice? Dances the finest? Makes the best food?
H3	Getting there
P	The Wandering Market is a <b>Fae domain</b> (page 102), made anew by a different host each time it convenes.
P	To find the market, one must know when it is happening and find an entrance. The entrances are many, but different each time.
P	Any Fae knows where the nearest entrance lies—pick or roll for the terrain near which it is found (page 202 for the <b>Great</b> <b>Wood</b>, page 118 for <b>Ferrier's Fen</b>), and pick some whimsical requirement such as:
B	Climb the seventh alder tree you find; it's up there
B	Blindfold yourself; follow the bird who calls your name
B	Lay a path of stones into the hollow of a tree; walk the path at sundown
B	Go to sleep in a patch of bluebells, and visit the market in your dreams
H3	Impressions
B	Sensory overload: crowds and barkers, silks and spices, perfumes, feathers and flowers, leering inhuman faces
B	Wonders for sale: distilled friendship, liquid silence, crystalline sorrow, etc.
B	Snide comments about how this Market pales to previous ones
B	Squeals of delight at your smile, your wry comment, your whistled tune
B	How long have you been here, again?
H3	Chance encounters
P	Pick or have someone roll the Die of Fate.
P	1d12 encounter
HR
P	1 A Fae in mismatched finery, selling stolen wares; rejects all offers
P	2 One Fae savagely beating a servant; not a single eyebrow raised
P	3 A kindly green fruit-seller implores the PCs to "sample" his wares
P	4 A troupe's bedazzling performance:
P	fireworks, illusions, bored onlookers
P	5 A crone selling fine futures, fates altered, prophecies (re)written
P	6 A hand (paw?) on your purse, deftly attempting to "trade"
P	7 A tiny sub-market, in a beehive or a stump; astir with bug-sized Fae
P	8 A scandalous, sensual revel in the street; stepped around by most
P	9 Talking beasts, glum Fae, holloweyed children, collared and chained
P	10 An insult; a challenge shouted; a crowd gathering to watch
P	11 Whispers and fuss as one of the <b>Four Chieftains</b> (page 111) pass by
P	12 The host's pavilion, thematic and grand, teeming with politics
PAGE	107
H2	Moves
HR
P	<b>TREASURE HUNT</b>
P	When you <b><i>scour the Wandering Market for</i></b> <b><i>a solution</i></b>, say what problem you're hoping to solve and roll +CHA: <b>on a 7+</b>, you find someone offering just the thing, and can Haggle for it. But before you do, <b>on a 10+</b>, you must first pick 1; <b>on a 7-9</b>, you must first pick 3:
B	Someone else is trying to buy it (or pretending to); you must Haggle with disadvantage
B	It's not actually a solution itself, but rather a way to acquire one
B	It's cursed, stolen, or otherwise dangerous to use or possess
B	To even find it, you've put yourself in some Fae's debt
HR
P	<b>HAGGLE</b>
P	When you <b><i>dicker with a Fae</i></b> (anywhere, not just in the Wandering Market), roll
P	+WIS. Roll with advantage if they like you, and disadvantage if they wish you ill. <b>On</b> <b>a 12+</b>, it costs but a pittance; <b>on a 10-11</b>, pick 1; <b>on a 7-9</b>, pick 2; <b>on a 6-</b>, pick 3:
B	The price is Value 2, at least
B	The price is irreplaceable, cherished, heartbreaking to lose
B	The price is not truly yours to pay
B	It involves a promise, condition, or obligation, sure to cause trouble
B	You end up beholden to them Whatever the price, you've either agreed to it or you've insulted the Fae and the deal is off. Work together to figure out exactly what happened. Reneging on the deal is certain to insult the Fae and/or put you in their <b>debt</b> (page 99).
TH	trade opportunities
P	If the PCs get a trade opportunity (from the Seasons Change move), the Fae might offer the following. The PCs still need to Haggle for it, though!
B	An impossible task, like a whole season's worth of work done in a night
B	A secret, a memory, an answer to a mystery, help with a sticky problem, etc.
B	Fantastical trade goods (Value 2 or 3): cloth-of-clouds, mead brewed from dreams, dyes of glamour, etc.
B	A <b>Fae artifact</b> (page 108)
B	An artifact of the <b>Green Lords</b> (page 216), the <b>Forest Folk</b> (page 154), the <b>spirits of the</b> <b>wild</b> (page 364), or perhaps the <b>Things Below</b> (page 424).

H3	Moonlight raiment
P	<i>magical</i>, <i>beautiful</i>, <i>fragile</i>
P	A gossamer robe, a joy against your skin.
P	When you <b><i>wear the raiment in dim light</i></b>, you become more pleasing to the eye. If normally ugly, you become plain. If plain, you become beautiful. If beautiful, you become luminous, breathtaking, magnificent.
P	Alas, when <b><i>the moonlight raiment is soiled</i></b> <b><i>or torn while you wear it</i></b>, mark a debility.
P	The debility cannot be cleared until the raiment is cleaned or repaired using Fae magic, or you burn it away into silvery ash.

E	an honest merchant touches them;
E	their current owner tells a lie;
E	someone sees through the glamour;
E	something dispels the glamour; or
E	the new moon comes and goes

H3	The Red Pennant
P	◇◇, <i>magical</i>, Blood A woolen flag hanging from a crossbar at the end of a sturdy long spear. It's tattered, crimson, with a crudely embroidered boot for a device. It hangs heavy. Like it's wet.
P	When you <b><i>fly the Red Pennant in battle</i></b>, all who fight on your side feel bloodlust boil within them. Hold 3 Blood. While the battle rages, you can spend Blood 1-for-1 to will your allies to:
B	Rush forward, driving back their foes
B	Hold fast, making their foes pay for every inch
B	Fight savagely, giving no quarter If spending Blood results in you Ordering
P	Followers or Deploying, or another PC
P	Clashing, the roll has advantage. Each time you spend Blood, those affected gain some small, animalistic or stony trait (little horns, weird eyes, crag-like wrinkles, etc.).
P	When you <b><i>spend the last Blood or the battle</i></b> <b><i>ends</i></b>, the Red Pennant's color fades and a few (~1 in 6) of those manifested traits will linger, especially in those who fought hardest. It will not function again until you soak it in the blood of fallen foes.
P	This is the battle standard of the <b>Bloody</b> <b>Boots</b> (page 112), their most sacred relic.
P	Don't expect them to just let it go.

H3	A sturdy, banded box
P	◇, <i>magical</i>
P	6" by 4" by 3", made of thick rowan wood and banded with bronze. It's not much to look at. It slips easily from one's mind.
P	When you <b><i>let a drop of your blood fall into</i></b> <b><i>the empty chest</i></b>, name a promise you have made, an oath you have given, or a debt that you owe. Your blood becomes a bead of lead as it falls into the chest, and the promise, oath, or debt holds no power over you as long as the chest is sealed.

H3	Auntie Sallow
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>large</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>magical</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>corrupted</i>, <i>terrifying</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 16; <b>Armor</b> 4 (resilience), 1 vs. iron (bark)
P	<b>Damage</b> choking fingers/tendrils d10+1 (<i>hand</i>, <i>close</i>, <i>reach</i>, <i>grabby</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities Fae nature</b> (page 98); takes +1d4 damage from bronze; leaches color from surroundings; knows whatever her moths know

P	• Find someone needing her "help"
P	• Show them their fears/nightmares
P	• Lure/drag them back to her home

P	Auntie Sallow is here to help."

P	Schemes and lies. Grief and endless pain.
P	'Twas in grief that <b>L'bin'bozia</b> (page 421) found her. Gave her the strength to help.
P	To find the innocent who suffered, the beautiful in despair. To offer succor, and the safety of her master's cool embrace.

H3	The Bear of Winter
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>huge</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>magical</i>, <i>hoarder</i>, <i>devious</i>, <i>fierce</i>, <i>terrifying</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 26; <b>Armor</b> 5 (resilience, ice), 2 vs. iron (hide, ice)
P	<b>Damage</b> bite or maul d12+5 (<i>close</i>, <i>hand</i>, <i>reach</i>, <i>forceful</i>, <i>grabby</i>, <i>messy</i>, 1 piercing)
P	<b>Special qualities Fae nature</b> (page 98); immune to cold; aura of wintry weather, matching his mood <b>Instinct</b> to protect his status and holdings
P	• Weave ice and snow, glamours and illusions, entire Fae domains
P	• Send a minion (spirit, beast, or indebted Fae) to do his bidding
P	• Wield the wintry elements
P	• Take the form of a scarred old man or a storm of sleet and snow
P	• Make use of a forgotten artifact
P	When winter snows blanket the Great Wood, the Bear roams the land. He's most often met as a great and snuffling beast, big as a house, icicles clinging to his fur. His retinue follows: nervously, discretely, waiting upon his call. He visits the many Fae who owe him favors and those who have pledged him their support. None are happy to see him. None dare turn him away.
P	The Bear, you see, is among the most powerful of the Fae. Snapped his own master's neck. Gobbled down its corpse. He freed hundreds of Fae from servitude. He leveraged the debts they owed him to become something of a feudal lord.
P	The Bear's domain is a great cave, full of hoarded riches and slinking servants. It has many entrances and exits, each leading to a different cave mouth in the world, but only when that cave mouth is surrounded by drifts of snow.
H2	The Four Chieftains
P	The chieftains are among the most powerful of the Fae, personally and politically. The Bear of Winter is one of them. The others might include:
B	<b>The Warbler</b>, who dwells in the springtime canopy and fills the world with song. An incorrigible gossip, who pretends to be a fool. Often goes incognito. Extremely well-informed.
B	<b>The Crowned Stag</b>, who troops through deep summer woods with their court and hangers-on. Beautiful, proud, dashing, and noble. Lusty, too, and prone to fall in love.
B	<b>Longshadow</b>, a stately old tree-wife, bare of leaves. Found brooding in the autumn forest, attended by skittish minions. Speaks prophecy, lays subtle plans. Knows that the war isn't over.

HR
ICON	icons/fae.svg
H3	Blush-of-Dawn
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>magical</i>, <i>beautiful</i>, <i>passionate</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 12; <b>Armor</b> 4 (resilience), 0 vs. iron <b>Damage</b> fiery touch d8 w/disadvantage (<i>hand</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities Fae nature</b> (page 98); radiant
P	<b>Instinct</b> to be adored
P	• Sing a song to stir the blood
P	• Inspire passion/jealousy/devotion
P	• Steal away into their Fae domain, perhaps with a new prize in tow
P	• Set devotees to a task/challenge
P	• Blaze brightly, blind onlookers
P	They were the shining jewel in some Green Lord's paradise, the bright beauty of a rising sun made flesh. They were happy and in love. (Or so they thought, for can a being bred to love truly do so?)
P	Then their master's tomb was plundered by the rebels. Their world was upended. They were bereft, vulnerable, alone and unloved.
P	They had no interest in freedom, only the safe warm surety of other beings' full regard. Fortunately, for them, such adoration was easy to find.
P	Their domain is a stately pavilion in a summer glade, forever in that moment just before the dawn. It's filled with fawning victims of their charms: lovers and would-be lovers, abducted children, devotees. And on the outskirts: the castout wretches, those who've lost favor but whose jealous adoration still feeds the Blush-of-Dawn.

H3	The Bloody Boots
P	<i>Group</i>, <i>small</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>ugly</i>, <i>violent</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 12; <b>Armor</b> 4 (resilience), 2 vs. iron <b>Damage</b> oversized club d8 w/advantage (<i>close</i>, <i>crude</i>) or iron-shod boots d8+2 w/advantage (<i>hand</i>, <i>forceful</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities Fae nature</b> (page 98); tolerates iron; can't start violence <b>Instinct</b> to brawl, the nastier the better
P	• Insult, mock, heap abuse
P	• Get in your face, dare you
P	• Leverage their unlikely strength
P	• Stomp someone who's down (<i>messy</i>)
P	A gang of hoodlums, with names like Hobnail, Spitkicker, Big Thunk, Tusk, and Grub.
P	Short, squat, brutes with lopsided limbs, mismatched parts, and craggy skin. They stomp about in oversized, iron-shod boots, delighting in the disgust of other Fae.
P	Back in the day, they quarried stone for their masters. Didn't even mind it much.
P	But given the chance to fight and brawl and spill all the blood they could, well, no need to ask them twice. The Bloody Boots were among the most feared and storied troops of the war. First into the fray and dyeing their <b>Red Pennant</b> (page 109) in the blood of trodden foes.
P	And after the war? Well, you can't have thugs like them just rampaging about.
P	Some little schemer bought and traded for every debt they ever had, then extracted a promise from each: no starting fights. They can finish a fight that someone else starts, and, oh, will they enjoy it. But just about every Fae still living knows better than to give them that chance.

H3	Hollow Fae
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>undead</i>, <i>confused</i>,
P	<i>terrifying</i>, see below
P	<b>HP</b> 19; <b>Armor</b> 5 (resilience, lacks vitals),
P	1 vs. black iron <b>Damage</b> life-drain d10 (<i>hand</i>, <i>close</i>, <i>area</i>, ignores armor)
P	<b>Special qualities</b> senses life; surrounded by inert death and ash; can be truly destroyed only by black iron
P	<b>Instinct</b> to consume life-force
P	• Moan, filling all with dread
P	• Tear apart Fae magic
P	• Pause in confusion when confronted with who it once was
P	• Open wide, drink in the vitality of the living (inflicting debilities)
P	A Fae wounded by <b>black iron</b> (page 307) will pray for death. For to survive such a wound is a curse. They grow weak, then confused, then hungry. Soon, they become a walking husk, surrounded by death, inhaling any source of life they find.
P	Hollow Fae are no longer vulnerable to mere iron or steel. Debts and promises no longer bind them. They will tear their way free of any Fae domain. Only black iron can destroy them, and what living Fae would be fool enough to try?
P	When faced with such a terror, most Fae choose to flee. A few might be so clever as to trap it in some forgotten tomb. But the cleverest, oh, the cleverest… they find some fool mortal to handle the problem for them.
P	A <i>large</i> Hollow Fae is tougher than shown above: 23 HP and +1 damage, +<i>reach</i>. A <i>huge</i> one is tougher still, with 27 HP, +3 damage, and +<i>reach</i>.

P	<i>Horde</i>, <i>tiny</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>magical</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>organized</i>

P	• Blend in, watch unseen

P	• Swarm a threat

P	Tiny little things, winged and fluttering, the size of mice or dragonflies. Weird little things, too: mishmashes of fur and feather, scales and chitin, gossamer and wings.
P	Beautiful, cute, or grotesque.

Or, if you're unlucky, you might encounter a gang of them out roaming the woods or fen, bored and cruel and looking for sport, and you'd be just the thing.

H3	The White Billies
P	<i>Horde</i>, <i>fae</i>, <i>athletic</i>, <i>raucous</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 7; <b>Armor</b> 4 (resilience), 0 vs. iron <b>Damage</b> headbutt d6+2 (<i>hand</i>, <i>forceful</i>)
P	<b>Special qualities Fae nature</b> (page 98) <b>Instinct</b> to suppress their grief
P	• Drag someone into their revels
P	• Get huffy if refused
P	• Lash out if forced to face the past
P	Muscular folk with cloven hooves, birchwhite fur, and horns in every size and shape.
P	They seem so happy, their endless days spent dancing and singing, drinking and rutting, indulging in good-natured brawls.
P	But when you look closer, you see the scars.
P	You see the missing limbs, the broken horns. You see, briefly, the eyes so full of pain. But, no, no, it's gone. Another dance!
P	Another round! Another bawdy song!
P	When you <b><i>join the White Billies in their</i></b> <b><i>revels</i></b>, lose 1d6 HP, mark a debility, and roll +CON: <b>on a 10+</b>, you keep your wits about you and learn something useful; <b>on</b> <b>a 7-9</b>, you regain your wits later, drunk and exhausted (mark another debility), with some new excess about to start; <b>on a 6-</b>, mark another debility and pick 1:
B	You've upset them; real violence is imminent
B	You come to later, alone, and who knows how long it's been
B	You're enthralled, reveling endlessly until someone rescues you
